# AMBROSIA: A Benchmark for Parsing Ambiguous Questions into Database Queries

[All reading notes](../reading-notes.md) · [Catalog entry](../README.md#ambrosia)

**Full paper read · 2026-11-09**

[Original source](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2406.19073v2) · arXiv:2406.19073v2, 31 October 2024; NeurIPS 2024 Datasets and Benchmarks paper

**Reading coverage:** All 29 PDF pages, including checklist and Appendices A-H: generation prompts, database configurations, annotation protocol, evaluation/extraction details, error examples and datasheet. Few-shot plot and annotation-interface figure visually inspected.

## Research question

Evaluate multiple valid SQL interpretations when linguistic ambiguity persists despite fully available database context.

## Method

Generates constrained synthetic databases, then elicits human questions and interpretations. Scope/attachment SQL comes from templates; vague-query SQL begins with expert-written queries on simplified schemas. Retains nonempty, distinct interpretation results.

## Evaluation

1,277 ambiguous questions, 2,965 resolved interpretations and 846 databases across 16 domains; 10% reserved for demonstrations. Six LLMs use ambiguity prompts or beam outputs with complete schema and data dumps. Micro recall, precision and AllFound score interpretation coverage.

## What the results support

Best zero-shot ambiguous recall is 30.7% and AllFound 1.9% for prompted Llama3-70B; its resolved-input recall is 64.5%. Few-shot examples modestly improve coverage. Attachment is difficult even when resolved, so parser capability also affects results.

## Limits and qualifications

Small synthetic databases and three ambiguity families limit realism. Matching flattens query output into sets of values, allowing occasional false equivalences. Interpretations can remain ambiguous; SQL-aware annotators and templates constrain language. No unanswerability or live clarification policy is evaluated.

## Relevance to reliable Text-to-SQL

Strong controlled test of interpretation coverage; combine with precision and resolved-input baselines rather than treating AllFound as complete dialogue success.

## Checks against the paper

These are interpretations checked against the source, not verbatim quotations attributed to its authors.

| Claim or inference examined | Original evidence | Location | Assessment |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Execution matching establishes semantic equivalence. | Appendix F represents output as a set of values, intentionally ignoring layout; it acknowledges possible false positives. | Appendix F, PDF page 20 | Describe relaxed single-database execution matching, not semantic proof. |
| Low ambiguous accuracy isolates ambiguity handling. | Attachment resolved-input recall is only 24.0% for prompted Llama3-70B, and Appendix G lists ordinary joins, filters, output-column and execution errors. | Table 3; Appendix G | Include resolved-input performance to separate parsing difficulty from ambiguity. |
| The evaluation covers arbitrary real-world databases and requests. | Databases have 3-5 rows per table on average; generation imposes seven configurations, filters empty results, and provides full database dumps. | Sections 3.3-4; Section 5; Appendices D and H | Retain controlled synthetic scope and explicit deployment limitations. |
